sources.bodyExcerpt: Big Muff Pi with Tone Wicker by Electro-Harmonix | RockBoard | PedalPedia Skip to main content LOG IN EXPLORE Electro-Harmonix Big Muff Pi with Tone Wicker LOG IN TO SUGGEST IMPROVEMENTS FUZZ Description The Big Muff Pi with Tone Wicker is a versatile fuzz and distortion pedal that expands upon the classic NYC Big Muff circuit by adding specialized tone-shaping toggles. The Wicker switch opens up three high-frequency filters to add top-end bite and rasp, while the Tone switch allows the user to bypass the tone control entirely for a raw, unfiltered broadband assault. When both switches are in their stock positions, the pedal delivers the legendary sustain and thick harmonic saturation characteristic of the original 1970s design. This model is housed in a compact XO-series die-cast chassis, making it more pedalboard-friendly than its predecessors. It is frequently utilized by musicians seeking the traditional "Muff" sound with increased clarity and presence in a modern format. sources.snippet: Electro-Harmonix Big Muff Pi with Tone Wicker Manual
sources.bodyExcerpt: Electro-Harmonix Big Muff Pi with Tone Wicker User Manual PDF | Manualsnet --> Electro-Harmonix Sustainer Big Muff Pi with Tone Wicker Manuals Electro-Harmonix Big Muff Pi with Tone Wicker Manual Pages 3 Year 0 Language(s) en Share PDF Preview Text Only Previous of 3 GO Next Previous of 3 GO Next Page 1 BIG MUFF PI WITH TONE WICKER With Enhanced Tone Processing Congratulations on your purchase of the BIG MUFF Pi with TONE WICKER! The BMPTW is a battery operated distortion pedal that maintains the legendary Big Muff Pi sound while offering two powerful and dynamic tonal adjustments that are unique to any distortion or fuzz product found in the market today. The original BIG MUFF PI sound is maintained while new tonal variations deliver edgy and aggressive sonic possibilities. - THEORY OF OPERATION - The BIG MUFF Pi with TONE WICKER is an effects pedal designed to deliver all of the sonic power of the legendary Big Muff Pi while providing user editing capabilities that are unique to the Tone Wicker design. Wicker mode opens up the high frequency bandwidth of your distortion sound delivering a top end that is new and exciting. The Tone switch, when set to OFF, defeats the Big Muffs Tone knob yielding an extremely powerful distortion with a fire breathing new Big Muff Pi character. - CONTROLS - Sustain knob As in the original Big Muff Pi, adjusts the amount of sustain and distortion. Tone Knob The Tone knob allows the musician to dial in just the right setting between deep bass and high treble. Volume Knob The volume knob sets the overall output level of the effect. Wicker Switch Activate Wicker mode by flipping the Wicker switch up to the ON position where the high frequency bandwidth is opened up for a bright and clear top end. Set the Wicker switch to OFF to obtain the classic Big Muff Pi sound. Page 2 Tone Switch The Tone switch allows the user to activate the Tone knob or to completely bypass the tone circuitry. When the Tone switch is set to ON, the Tone knob is active, just like a standard Big Muff. When the Tone switch is set to OFF, the Tone knob and all of its circuitry is bypassed. This setting yields a totally new Muff distortion with a powerful drive and uncolored gain. High output with attitude. Please Note: When the Tone switch is set to OFF, turning the Tone knob will produce no change to your sound. In addition, it is normal for the output volume of your Big Muff Pi with Tone Wicker to increase when moving the Tone switch from ON to OFF. Status LED - When the LED is lit; the BMPTW effect is active. When the LED is off, the BMPTW is in True Bypass mode. The Footswitch toggles between effect and bypass modes. INPUT Jack This jack is the audio input to the BMPTW. The input impedance presented at this jack is 130 k. OUTPUT Jack This jack is the audio output from the BMPTW. When the BMPTW is in Bypass mode, the OUTPUT jack is connected directly to the INPUT jack. 9V Power Jack The Big Muff with Tone Wicker is battery powered. You may use an external AC Adapter power supply instead of the battery. Connect the AC Adapters plug to the 9V Power Jack at the top of the BMPTW. The power jacks polarity is center negative. The BMPTW requires a clean 9VDC power supply at 50mA. We recommend the Electro-Harmonix US96DC-200BI power supply. - WARRANTY INFORMATION - Please register online at http://www.ehx.com/product-registration or complete and return the enclosed warranty card within 10 days of purchase. Electro-Harmonix will repair or replace, at its discretion, a product that fails to operate due to defects in materials or workmanship for a period of one year from date of purchase. This applies only to original purchasers who have bought their product from an authorized Electro-Harmonix retailer. Repaired or replaced units will then be warranted for the unexpired portion of the original warranty term. A unique design from a Milwaukee audio repair shop in the 1970s, the original is rare, gooped, and has gained a cult-classic status. The EHX Percolator expands on this original by adding modern control to a seriously wild sounding pedal. The basis of the pedal’s tone ranges from raunchy overdrive tones to ripping heavy fuzz. These sounds are achieved by asymmetrical clipping emphasizing even-order harmonics creating an interactive tonal experience that reacts to your playing dynamics musically with the potential for absolutely explosive tones. The EHX Percolator includes a simple but effective control set of three knobs and a single switch yielding a near infinite possibility of sounds from sweet and gentle, to face-rippingly fierce. HARMONICS controls the input gain of the pedal from overdrive to complete fuzz destruction. The BIAS control sets the bias of the gain circuit, creating sounds from smooth drive to pseudo-octave fuzz to Velcro gated fuzz tones. BALANCE sets the overall output of the effect. The DRIVE/FUZZ toggle engages the clipping diodes in FUZZ position for heavy fuzz sounds. While in DRIVE mode with the diodes disengaged, the EHX Percolator acts more like a transistor drive pedal with a raw, organic character that’s both chewy and crunchy. Under the hood, an internal trim pot can be adjusted to further enhance and bring out the sub-octave while also adding even more gain to the circuit for massive distortion with extra rumble. The EHX Percolator features True Bypass and a footswitch with Latching/Momentary action. Clicking the footswitch produces a normal latching function. A press and hold of the footswitch results in a momentary change between bypass states for a burst of fuzz and an instant change back to bypass when you lift your foot, or vice versa. Check out the leaked $99 EHX Percolator, a modern, high-gain upgrade to the iconic 1970s Interfax circuit Jef Stone · Jun 15, 2026 Contains affiliate links The gear world is buzzing following a major retailer leak revealing that Electro-Harmonix is poised to launch the EHX Percolator . Clocking in at an incredibly accessible $99 price point , this upcoming analog stompbox is a highly modernized, feature-packed tribute to the mythical 1970s Interfax Harmonic Percolator. Melding the untamed gain of a vintage fuzz with the articulate string-to-string definition of a premium overdrive, the EHX variant is already positioning itself to be one of the most anticipated pedal releases of the year. For experimental players, noise-rock aficionados, and tone chasers looking for the best new fuzz pedals, this surprise addition to the EHX lineup promises boutique tones without the boutique price tag. UPDATE 16/06/25 The EHX Percolator is now officially released, priced at $99! Available at Guitar Center Available at Sweetwater Available at Thomann A History of Distortion: The Cult of the Harmonic Percolator To understand the immense hype surrounding the upcoming Electro-Harmonix Percolator, one must travel back to late-1970s Milwaukee. Genius electrical engineer Ed Giese designed the original HP-1 Harmonic Percolator at his "Cream City" audio repair shop, Interfax. Giese engineered a highly unique, asymmetrical clipping circuit utilizing an idiosyncratic combination of germanium and silicon transistors. This specific configuration was designed to intentionally emphasize even-order harmonics—the sweet, musical overtones naturally produced by cranked tube amplifiers. Though a true masterpiece of engineering, the original tan-and-brown units with their dual-slider layout were produced in incredibly limited numbers, quickly fading into obscurity. Steve Albini That was until underground rock icon Steve Albini —the legendary guitarist for Shellac and Rapeman, and the revered audio engineer behind Nirvana’s In Utero and Pixies’ Surfer Rosa —catapulted the pedal into legendary cult status. Albini famously deployed the Interfax original to sculp his signature abrasive, metallic, feedback-laden walls of sound. For Albini, the pedal was a secret weapon that defied traditional fuzz behavior; he famously noted that when the effect was engaged, "the guitar plays itself." Because original units became nearly impossible to find, commanding astronomical prices on the vintage market, the circuit became a holy grail for DIY builders and boutique clone manufacturers. Now, EHX is bringing that exact magic mainstream. EHX Percolator What we know (some information may be incorrect at the time of writing) until this new EHX Percolator pedal is officially released. EHX Percolator Key Features Expanded Controls While the vintage Interfax box was notoriously simple—sporting just two sliders for Harmonics and Balance—the EHX Percolator Fuzz/Overdrive Pedal expands the topology dramatically for modern pedalboards: Harmonics: Controls the input-stage gain, seamlessly transitioning from gritty, textured overdrive to saturated fuzz destruction. Bias: Pushes the gain circuit's bias into experimental territories, serving up spitting pseudo-octave tones and gated, sputtering "Velcro" fuzz. sources.h1: The EHX Percolator is a modern take on one of the rarest fuzz pedals ever made
sources.description: Electro-Harmonix's EHX Percolator is a modern take on the rare Interfax Harmonic Percolator, with added Bias control and FUZZ/DRIVE switch.
sources.snippet: The EHX Percolator is a modern take on one of the rarest fuzz pedals ...
sources.bodyExcerpt: EHX launch the Percolator – a circuit brought back from obscurity READING The EHX Percolator is a modern take on one of the rarest fuzz pedals ever made Subscribe X Subscribe to Mixdown Magazine Select State NSW QLD VIC ACT TAS SA WA NT --> Subscribe News Features Reviews Directory Giveaways Videos Magazines Privacy & Policies Advertise Contact Terms & Conditions News Product 17.06.2026 The EHX Percolator is a modern take on one of the rarest fuzz pedals ever made Words by Mixdown The new pedal brings Steve Albini's favourite fuzz drive back from obscurity, now with a Bias control and FUZZ/DRIVE switch. The Interfax Harmonic Percolator is one of those pedals most players only really encounter in gear forums and Steve Albini interviews. Now, Electro-Harmonix has built a version of it. Catch up on all the latest news here. EHX’s modern take on the incredibly rare Interfax Harmonic Percolator – an old-school fuzz drive famously used by Steve Albini on stage and in the studio –is the EHX Percolator. Based on the same even-order harmonic clipping circuit as the Interfax, it covers ground from overdriven crunch to heavier fuzz territory. HARMONICS sets the input gain, BALANCE sets output level, and the added Bias control adjusts the gain stage bias to dial in gated sounds and enhanced sub-octave content, none of which was available on the original. The FUZZ/DRIVE switch is the other addition. FUZZ mode runs standard clipping for heavier fuzz tones; DRIVE lifts the diodes for a transistor-style drive character that’s rawer and more open. All four controls interact with each other, so the range of sounds available is wider than the control count suggests. The footswitch doubles as latching and momentary. A quick click toggles it on or off as normal, and holding it down engages the effect only for as long as your foot is on the switch, dropping back to bypass the moment you lift it off – handy for a quick burst of fuzz mid-song. See the pedal in action here: The Percolator ships with a 9V battery and is available now. For local enquiries on EHX, head here . sources.bodyExcerpt: ELECTRO-HARMONIX EHX PERCOLATOR OPERATING INSTRUCTIONS Pdf Download | ManualsLib Sign In Upload Download Add to my manuals Delete from my manuals Share URL of this page: HTML Link: ELECTRO-HARMONIX EHX PERCOLATOR OPERATING INSTRUCTIONS Pdf Download '> Pinterest Bookmark this page Add Manual will be automatically added to "My Manuals" Print this page × Bookmark added × Added to my manuals Manuals Brands Electro-Harmonix Manuals Music Pedal EHX Percolator Operating instructions Electro-Harmonix EHX Percolator Operating Instructions Hide thumbs 1 2 3 page of 3 Go / 3 Bookmarks Quick Links Download this manual Welcome to the Electro Harmonix EHX Percolator, a unique take on distortion and fuzz that emphasizes even-order harmonics to enhance your tone. Use the Harmonics knob to brighten and distort your instrument for a rich and clean distortion. Sculpt the sound further with the Bias knob to create octave-like fuzz tones or intense gated fuzz effects. The Drive/Fuzz switch engages the clipping diodes to further enhance the fuzz tone. Equally potent on both guitar and bass, the EHX Percolator is a must have for tone and fuzz enthusiasts. Connect your instrument to the Input jack of the EHX Percolator and the Amp jack to your amp's input. Set the knobs to 50% and the toggle switch to the Fuzz position. Power EHX Percolator with a 9V battery or external 9VDC power supply. Press the footswitch to ensure the LED is lit. Your EHX Percolator is now ready to play. Voltage: 9VDC This device may be powered by an Electro-Harmonix 9.6DC-200, MOP-D10, or S8 power supply. It may also be powered with a 9V battery. Use of the wrong adapter or a plug with the wrong polarity may damage the device and void the warranty. Do not exceed 12VDC on the power plug. Power supplies rated for less than 50mA can cause the device to act unreliably. The Electro-Harmonix Germanium OD is a vintage overdrive pedal based on a hand-selected germanium transistor. This classic 1960's overdrive pedal is designed to deliver exceptional vintage overdrive tones. The pedal features three main controls: Gain, Bias, and Volts. The Gain control adjusts the amount of input signal fed to the pedal, affecting the intensity of the overdrive. The Bias control adjusts the current gain sent to the germanium transistor, working in conjunction with the Volts control to shape the overall tone. The Volts control allows the user to adjust the amount of voltage applied to the pedal, allowing for a variety of saturation levels and tone variations. The Germanium OD also features a Status LED that indicates when the effect is active, as well as a footswitch for engaging and disengaging the pedal. sources.bodyExcerpt: Electro-Harmonix Germanium OD Overdrive User Manual PDF | Manualsnet --> Electro-Harmonix OverDrive Germanium OD Manuals Electro-Harmonix Germanium OD Manual Pages 3 Year 0 Language(s) en Share PDF Preview Text Only Previous of 3 GO Next Previous of 3 GO Next Page 1 GERMANIUM OD Vintage Overdrive The Electro-Harmonix GERMANIUM OD is a classic 1960s overdrive based around a hand selected germanium transistor. To get the best results from it please set aside some time to practice in a quiet roomjust you, your amp, and the Germaium OD. The interaction of each control will reward you with many different flavors of exceptional vintage overdrive. -CONTROLS- GAIN CONTROL Adjusts the amount of input signal that is fed to the GERMANIUM OD. The more the knob is rotated the harder the Germanium transistor and drive components are hit. BIAS CONTROL Adjusts the current gain that is sent to the Germanium transistor. It works together with the voltage control to attain the over all tone. The bias control works specifically with the Germanium transistor. VOLTS CONTROL Allows the user to control the amount of voltage that is applied to the GERMANIUM OD. When the knob is set at full, 9volts is applied. When set at minimum 3 volts of current is applied By limiting the volts applied to the pedal a number of interesting saturations can be set up for variations in tone. STATUS LED When the LED is lit; the GERMANIUM OD effect is active. When the LED is off, the Germanium OD is in True Bypass Mode. The footswitch engages/disengages the effect. INPUT Jack Connect your instrument to the input jack. The input impedance presented at the input jack is high. OUTPUT Jack Connect this jack to your amplifier. This is the GERMANIUM OD output. This jack is connected directly to the Input Jack. Footswitch --True Bypass on and off. Page 2 9V Power Jack The GERMANIUM OD can run off of a 9V battery or you can connect a 9VDC battery eliminator capable of delivering at least 100mA to the 9V power jack. The optional 9V power supply from Electro-Harmonix is 9.6DC-200BI (same as used by Boss Ibanez) 9.6 Volts DC 200mA. The battery eliminator must have a barrel connector with center negative. The battery may be left in or taken out when using an eliminato r. -OPERATING INSTRUCTIONS and HINTS- The BIAS KNOB: Experiment with this control. You will notice differences in reaction as the current to the Germanium transistor varies. The VOLTS KNOB should normally be set to 9 volts but as you back off between 3 o clock and 9 o clock you are lowering the number of volts applied to the germanium transistor. Totally different reactions in the sound can be obtained. The GAIN KNOB is the master output volume for the GERMANIUM OD. - POWER - Plugging into the INPUT jack activates power from the internal 9-volt battery. The input cable should be removed when the unit is not in use to avoid running down the battery. If a battery eliminator is used, the Germanium OD will be powered as long as a wall-wart is plugged into the wall. To change the 9-volt battery, you must remove the 4 screws on the bottom of the Germanium OD. Once the screws are removed, you can take off the bottom plate and change the battery. Please do not touch the circuit board while the bottom plate is off or you risk damaging a component. - WARRANTY INFORMATION - Please register online at http://www.ehx.com/product-registration or complete and return the enclosed warranty card within 10 days of purchase. Electro- Harmonix will repair or replace, at its discretion, a product that fails to operate due to defects in materials or workmanship for a period of one year from date of purchase. This applies only to original purchasers who have bought their product from an authorized Electro-Harmonix retailer. Repaired or replaced units will then be warranted for the unexpired portion of the original warranty term. A little background… the sample rate is the number of times per second that a sample or snapshot of an analog signal is taken. For example, CDs (remember them?) had a sample rate of 44.1kHz which means that the original analog signal is sampled 44,100 times per second. The sample rate defines the frequency range that can be reproduced while maintaining good fidelity. When the sample rate is reduced the quality of the audio is degraded and aliasing occurs. Aliasing means audible artifacts created when higher frequencies are sampled at an inadequate rate and the result is distortion. The Mainframe’s sample rate range is wide enough to take you from sounds that are quite pristine to sounds that are unrecognizable when compared to the input signal. It also provides bit crushing ranging from 24-bit to 1-bit. What does that mean? Bit crushing is bit depth reduction. Back to our CD example… CDs used a 16-bit bit depth meaning that each of its samples was represented by 16-bits of information. Higher bit depths can accurately represent a greater dynamic range while bit crushing increases the number of sampling errors and creatively degrades the sound to bring us back to those nasty “old school” sounds we love. The Mainframe’s selectable High/Low/Band-Pass filter lets the user shape the artifacts of the bit crushing and sample rate. Another very cool feature is its Sample Rate Tuning Mode where the pedal analyzes your input signal in real-time and sets the sample rate to match the pitch of your signal, or a set interval above your signal. sources.description: Electro-Harmonix has unveiled the Mainframe—a dual-engine, 128-preset, stereo multi-effects processor with full MIDI implementation, USB-C audio interface capabilities, and a unique 'Pedalboard Mode' for seamless integration with external pedals. This article examines its architecture, real-world usability in teaching environments, latency benchmarks (0.87 ms analog path, 2.3 ms DSP processing), and how its programmable expression inputs and IR loader transform rehearsal, composition, and student assessment workflows.

sources.bodyExcerpt: Electro-Harmonix Announces The Mainframe: A Deep Technical and Pedagogical Analysis for Guitar Educators and Practicing Musicians | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / practice tips practice tips Electro-Harmonix Announces The Mainframe: A Deep Technical and Pedagogical Analysis for Guitar Educators and Practicing Musicians By Liam Carter July 23, 2026 What Is the Electro-Harmonix Mainframe—and Why It Matters for Music Education Electro-Harmonix has officially launched the Mainframe: a compact, rack-mountable (1U, 482 mm wide × 44 mm high × 215 mm deep), dual-DSP multi-effects processor designed explicitly for professional guitarists, studio engineers, and—critically—music educators. Unlike conventional floor-based multi-FX units, the Mainframe features two independent signal paths (A and B), each with its own dedicated 32-bit floating-point SHARC ADSP-21489 DSP running at 400 MHz, delivering sub-2.5 ms total processing latency. With 128 onboard presets, full USB-C bidirectional audio/MIDI (supporting class-compliant 24-bit/96 kHz operation), and native support for impulse response (IR) loading via SD card or computer, it redefines what’s possible in both live performance and pedagogical settings. Its built-in 8-channel USB audio interface enables direct recording into DAWs like Ableton Live 12, Logic Pro 13, and Reaper 7 without additional hardware. For music educators managing diverse student skill levels—from beginner chord progressions to advanced modal interchange studies—the Mainframe’s granular parameter control, snapshot switching, and real-time expression mapping offer unprecedented flexibility in lesson design and auditory feedback delivery. Architectural Innovation: Dual Signal Paths and True Stereo Processing The Mainframe’s core innovation lies in its true dual-path architecture. Each path—labeled A and B—operates independently with its own complete effects chain: preamp, distortion, modulation, delay, reverb, and output EQ. This isn’t merely parallel routing; it’s simultaneous, sample-accurate processing with zero crosstalk. Both paths accept mono or stereo input and can be routed to mono, stereo, or dual-mono outputs. Crucially, the unit supports three operational modes: Split (e.g., clean rhythm on Path A, lead overdrive on Path B), Blend (crossfading between two tonal palettes), and Series (Path A feeding directly into Path B for cascaded effects like chorus → tape delay → convolution reverb). This architecture allows instructors to build pedagogically intentional signal chains—for instance, assigning Path A to demonstrate standard jazz comping tones (Fender Twin IR + subtle rotary speaker + 600 ms stereo delay), while Path B models a contemporary indie-rock verse sound (low-gain TS9 emulation + pitch-shifted shimmer reverb + dynamic tremolo). Hardware Specifications That Enable Precision Teaching Measuring precisely 482 mm × 44 mm × 215 mm (19″ rack width, 1U height), the Mainframe fits seamlessly into standard educational AV racks alongside Behringer X32 consoles or Focusrite Scarlett 18i20 interfaces. Its rear panel includes: two balanced XLR inputs (20 dBu max, 10 MΩ impedance), two balanced XLR outputs (20 dBu max), two unbalanced ¼” instrument-level inputs (1 MΩ), two unbalanced ¼” outputs, MIDI In/Out/Thru (5-pin DIN), USB-C (for audio, MIDI, firmware updates, and SD card backup), and an SD card slot supporting up to 128 GB microSDXC cards. Power is supplied via included 12 V DC, 2.5 A adapter (center-negative, 2.1 mm × 5.5 mm barrel). Internal thermal management uses passive aluminum heatsinks—no fans—ensuring silent classroom operation. The front-panel OLED display (128 × 64 pixels) renders parameter names, values, and waveform visualizations in high contrast, even under stage lighting or fluorescent classroom conditions. sources.description: A precise, measurement-backed evaluation of the Electro-Harmonix Nano Bass Big Muff Pi — covering its circuit topology, frequency response (60 Hz–1.2 kHz fundamental emphasis), gain staging, noise floor (measured at -72.4 dBu RMS), pedalboard footprint (3.85" × 2.25" × 1.4" / 98 × 57 × 36 mm), and real-world performance with Fender Precision Bass, Music Man StingRay 5, and passive vs. active pickup configurations.

sources.bodyExcerpt: Quick Hit: Electro-Harmonix Nano Bass Big Muff Pi Review — Tone, Design, and Practical Use for Bassists | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / music theory music theory Quick Hit: Electro-Harmonix Nano Bass Big Muff Pi Review — Tone, Design, and Practical Use for Bassists By Marcus Reeve July 20, 2026 The Electro-Harmonix Nano Bass Big Muff Pi is not merely a downsized relic—it’s a purpose-built distortion engine optimized for low-end integrity, dynamic headroom, and pedalboard efficiency. Unlike generic bass overdrives or repurposed guitar fuzzes, this pedal employs a discrete transistor-based clipping stage derived from EHX’s 2012 Bass Big Muff Pi, modified for tighter low-mid control and reduced subsonic mud. Measuring precisely 3.85 inches wide × 2.25 inches deep × 1.4 inches tall (98 × 57 × 36 mm) and weighing 228 grams, it fits comfortably alongside a Boss TU-3, MXR Micro Amp, and Fulltone OCD in a standard 12-space pedalboard layout. Its measured noise floor sits at −72.4 dBu RMS (A-weighted, input terminated at 1 kΩ), significantly quieter than the vintage Sovtek Muff (−65.1 dBu) and comparable to the Darkglass B7K Ultra (−73.8 dBu). In practice, it delivers articulate growl from 60 Hz fundamentals up through 1.2 kHz harmonics—preserving note definition even at 85% Sustain and full Tone. This review dissects its architecture, tonal behavior across instrument types, power requirements, and measurable interactions with common bass rigs—including direct recording chains and tube preamps. Origins and Circuit Philosophy Electro-Harmonix introduced the original Bass Big Muff Pi in 2012 as a direct response to bassists’ frustration with guitar-oriented fuzz pedals collapsing below 120 Hz. The design team—led by engineer Zachary Vex—revised the classic four-transistor Big Muff topology by replacing the first two silicon transistors (2N5088) with higher-gain, lower-noise MPSA18 devices and widening the coupling capacitor between stages from 0.01 µF to 0.1 µF. This extended low-frequency response and reduced phase shift below 80 Hz. The Nano version, released in 2019, retains that core signal path but implements surface-mount components, a revised PCB layout, and a simplified power regulation scheme. Crucially, it omits the buffered bypass found in the full-size model—opting instead for true hard-wire bypass with a mechanical footswitch (not relay-based). This preserves transient fidelity but introduces a slight high-end roll-off (−1.3 dB at 8 kHz) when disengaged, verified via Audio Precision APx555 testing. Transistor Selection and Clipping Behavior The Nano Bass Big Muff Pi uses three discrete NPN transistors per channel: two MPSA18s in the pre-clipping gain stage and one 2N5088 in the final clipping stage. Unlike op-amp-based distortions (e.g., the Tech 21 SansAmp Bass Driver DI), this all-transistor design generates asymmetric soft clipping rich in even-order harmonics—particularly strong at the 2nd (120 Hz for a low E) and 4th (240 Hz) partials. Oscilloscope analysis shows clipping onset begins at +1.8 dBu input level, with full saturation reached at +8.2 dBu—a 6.4 dB headroom window ideal for dynamic playing. When fed a 60 Hz sine wave at line level (−10 dBV), harmonic distortion measures THD+N = 12.7% at 3 o’clock Sustain, rising to 28.3% at maximum Sustain—yet maintains fundamental amplitude within ±0.4 dB, confirming exceptional low-end retention. Power Architecture and Current Draw This pedal operates exclusively on 9 V DC center-negative power (no battery option), drawing a steady 14.2 mA under load—well within the capacity of most modern isolated power supplies like the Voodoo Lab Pedal Power 2+ (which allocates 250 mA per port) or the Strymon Zuma (200 mA/port). It lacks reverse-polarity protection diodes, meaning incorrect adapter connection will damage the internal 78L09 voltage regulator. It’s super versatile and ready for your axe be it guitar, bass or keys. The Nano Overlord is switchable between two modes: Normal and Boost. Normal mode provides low to medium gain sounds and relies on three amp-like JFET gain stages. When Boost mode is engaged it’s like adding a pedal-type OD circuit in front of the JFET stages to really increase overall distortion. The pedal also features a Dry blend control which is invaluable for bass and keyboards, a 3-position input level selector switch and an active 3-band EQ. Tone aficionados kept telling Mike Matthews about a pedal that had achieved a lot of buzz because it was only obtainable at an exorbitant price. That pedal was the Klon Centaur. A believer in bringing great tools to starving musicians, Mike tasked his trusty team to create an affordable alternative, and that is how the EHX Soul Food Transparent Overdrive was cooked up. Its circuitry features boosted power rails to provide abundant headroom and increased definition. Best of all, you don’t have to be a rock star to own one! Specs, tone recipes, and buying guide inside. admin 22 September 2026 21 min read GG-ARTICLE-TOP There is a moment in the late summer of 1969 — Woodstock just finished, the counterculture at its peak — where a young guitarist walks into Manny’s Music on West 48th Street in New York City and picks up one of the first pedals Electro-Harmonix has ever placed in a retail store. That guitarist is Jimi Hendrix. He takes the Big Muff home. Shortly after, Mike Matthews — EHX founder — gets an invitation to hang out at a recording session. When he arrives, the Big Muff is sitting on the floor, plugged in. That is a primary-source confirmation from the man who built the pedal and witnessed the scene, documented in a Guitar World feature published September 2020. It does not get more authoritative than that. GG-ARTICLE-AFTER-INTRO The pedal on that floor was what we now call the Triangle Big Muff Pi: the original V1 circuit, named for the triangular layout of its three knobs — Volume, Sustain, Tone — arranged in a wide arc across a simple metallic chassis with plain black lettering. No ram’s head graphic. No color scheme. Just the circuit that started one of the longest-running fuzz dynasties in guitar history. EHX reissued this original circuit in 2018 to mark the company’s 50th anniversary. Mike Matthews himself explained the decision: “The Big Muff Pi is the pedal we are best known for so I wanted to commemorate EHX’s 50th Anniversary by re-releasing V1, the very first Big Muff. Original pedals are now selling for hundreds of dollars and this reissue absolutely nails that creamy, violin-like sustain and musical tone at a price a working musician can afford.” The Triangle Big Muff Pi reissue lives in the same compact nano-sized die-cast chassis used across EHX’s current lineup, with the same analog circuit inside and one key modern upgrade: true bypass switching. This is the one that started it all. Jump to the Rig ↓ How to Get the Tone ↓ The First Muff: From Workshop to Woodstock (1969–1972) The Big Muff Pi did not appear from nowhere. Mike Matthews had been working with fuzz circuits since the late 1960s, having taken over Guild’s Foxey Lady fuzz production — a two-transistor design — and selling it through Electro-Harmonix from 1968. But the Foxey Lady was a relatively simple circuit with limited sustain range. What Matthews wanted next was something richer, more sustained, more controllable. Learn more Featured Deal Save $100 on an exclusive Olive Green Line 6 HX Stomp Claim Reviews Electro-Harmonix Triangle Big Muff Pi Review A recreation of a vintage classic released in celebration of Electro-Harmonix’s 50th anniversary. by Michael Watts December 20, 2018 by Michael Watts December 20, 2018 When you purchase through affiliate links on Guitar.com, you may contribute to our site through commissions. Learn more Review Overview Our rating 9 Our verdict + The one vintage Muff fans have been waiting for ⊕ Great classic-rock fuzz tones ⊖ It will turn your extended chord voicings to mush. Just like the original! We’ve waited years for EHX to add to its selection of Nano-format Big Muffs, and then all of a sudden three have turned up in very quick succession. We checked out the Green Russian and the Op-Amp (designed in conjunction with Billy Corgan) previously, and now we have this – a faithful recreation of the pedal that started it all, the venerable Triangle Big Muff Pi, named after the positioning of the three control knobs on the original design. Originally released in 1969 as a logical progression from the existing Muff Fuzz, the Big Muff has become legendary for its ability to produce cello-like sustain for lead sounds, huge bass response for powerchord work and all manner of chaos and aggression for the more experimental player. The Big Muff tends to work best in partnership with an amp with a bit of midrange to show it to its full advantage and for this review, a hand-wired Vox AC4 was pressed into service. In use With the amp grumbling on the edge and a P-90-loaded SG in hand we set all three knobs on the Triangle Muff to 12 o’clock and hit the switch. An open E chord immediately summons up that familiar Big Muff roar with (as expected) most of the chord itself disappearing into a low-string powerchord. Such is the nature of the beast – indeed, anyone looking to hear every note in their major 7th and minor 9th chords may be shopping in the wrong department. This is, however, a classic Big Muff sound. A very good one, too. With more of a vintage feel than the Green Russian and Op-Amp offerings, this pedal covers some very pleasing classic-rock bases, from Python Lee Jackson top-fret histrionics to mid-period Mick Ronson-isms and, with the sustain dialled down a little and the tone up, it also does a convincing Samba Pa Ti . With the front pickup selected and the tone rolled off, we have a very vocal lead tone which, while it would require a boost to get it through a band mix on stage, is particularly addictive. Perhaps the most noteworthy proponent of vintage Big Muff tones is, of course, David Gilmour. And you’ll be relieved to hear that the Triangle Big Muff Pi proves itself to be very much at home in a psychedelic-rock scenario. Indeed with the addition of some vintage-sounding delay, reverb and flange it becomes pretty otherworldly, with soaring high bends and growling bass notes. It is perhaps in this context that the Triangle Big Muff Pi will find most favour. With myriad boutique pedal companies flooding Instagram with the promise of authentic vintage Muff tones at prices on a par with original vintage units, it is extremely encouraging to see Electro-Harmonix reminding the world of what it does best: characterful, musical and inspiring stompboxes at price-points that allow everyone to get a slice. Happy birthday EHX, and thanks for all the fuzz. Key Features  PRICE £93 DESCRIPTION True-bypass fuzz pedal powered by 9V battery or mains PSU CONTROLS Volume, sustain, tone, bypass switch DIMENSIONS 70 x 115 x 54mm CONTACT Electro-Harmonix ehx.com Michael Watts Michael is a guitarist, writer, educator, host and film

sources.title: Greathammer Bass Driver — Electronic Audio Experiments
sources.description: The Greathammer is a bass drive and preamp. Built upon an homage to a beloved solid state bass amplifier, it delivers noise rock thunder with key augmentations for the modern bassist.
sources.snippet: Greathammer Bass Driver — Electronic Audio Experiments
sources.bodyExcerpt: Greathammer Bass Driver — Electronic Audio Experiments Pedals Accessories DIY Dealers Blog Support About Menu Pedals Accessories DIY Dealers Blog Support About × Filter All Pedals ← Back to Pedals Greathammer Greathammer $249.00 The Electronic Audio Experiments Greathammer is a bass-focused overdrive that brings a distinct flavor of solid state thunder. With a gain control spanning a 50dB range, the Greathammer can be restrained or rowdy. We took cues from a beloved 1970s Canadian bass amplifier, but we did not shy away from redesigning entire circuit blocks from scratch. Without taking away the classic piano-like attack that defined 90s noise rock, we expanded the tonal range to suit more tasteful playing or filthy, down-tuned mayhem. Critically, our circuit can achieve far deeper low frequency extension than its progenitors—all without the unnatural, disconnected feel of a traditional clean blend. The Greathammer is equally effective in front of an amplifier or as a dedicated preamp. And, while we designed this with bass as a primary focus, it is quite striking on guitar as well. Color: Select Color Gray Acid Etch Gray Acid Etch Quantity: Add To Cart Electrical Specifications Bypass switching: Silent electronic switching with a high-headroom op amp buffer Input impedance @ 1Khz: 1MΩ Output impedance @ 1Khz: <1KΩ Power: 9VDC, 2.1mm center negative barrel. The current draw is 70mA . We recommend a regulated, isolated power supply rated for 100 mA minimum. The DC input is protected against reverse polarity and over-voltage up to 20V. Our pedals do not accept batteries. All Greathammer pedals come with our standard warranty. Download Manual (v1) Controls Level: overall volume level, capable of extremely high output Gain: signal gain, from clean to moderate to extreme. Approximately 50dB maximum passband gain. Bass: post-clipping low frequency shelf boost, up to +14db at 100Hz and below Attack: pre-gain tone control, adjusts frequencies above 1kHz to tailors the overall drive response and sharpness of pick attack Notch (toggle): 3-position mid cut. Center is a full mid cut, down is a moderate mid cut, and up is flat mids. Footswitch: Activates the effect with intelligent momentary/latching behavior. Changelog Version 1 Original release, January 2026 Sound Clips All clips recorded with an Ampeg V4 into a Greenboy Dually 2x15 cab with an Electrovoice RE20 approximately 2” off axis. The Greathammer is an update to the 0xEAE Bass Driver, originally released in Spring 2025. For this version we updated the circuit to fit in our standard pedalboard-friendly form factor, and we moved the previously internal Notch switch to the exterior. Page 3: Power And I/O 30 seconds or longer between power cycles to give the filter capacitors time to discharge. Use standard 1/4” patch cables to patch your Greathammer into a pedal chain, as normal. The input jack is on the top right and the output jack is on the top left. This pedal works anywhere in a signal chain. Page 4 3 Controls 4 Controls The controls are listed below. Refer to the next section for a more detailed guide. Level overall volume level, capable of extremely high output. Gain signal gain, from clean to moderate to extreme. Approximately 50dB maximum pass- band gain, with a slight low frequency contour at maximum. Page 5 5 Detailed Operating Instructions The Greathammer is designed to be a versatile gain device for bass, with a variety of use cases. Most folks will probably use it as an overdrive pedal in front of an amp, so we will start there and discuss other use cases below. sources.bodyExcerpt: Greathammer by Electronic Audio Experiments | RockBoard | PedalPedia Skip to main content LOG IN EXPLORE Electronic Audio Experiments Greathammer LOG IN TO SUGGEST IMPROVEMENTS OVERDRIVE PREAMP Description The Electronic Audio Experiments Greathammer is an all-analog, solid-state drive and preamp designed primarily for bass guitar but highly effective for guitar applications. It is a modern evolution of the "tri-comp" transistor clipping circuit found in the 1970s Traynor TS50B amplifier, famous for its sharp, piano-like attack and aggressive grind. Unlike the original amplifier, this circuit features a redesigned post-clipping active shelving filter for the Bass control, allowing for deep low-end extension without affecting the distortion character. An Attack control manages pre-gain frequencies to tailor the sharpness of pick strikes and clarity. The pedal also includes a three-position toggle for mid-range sculpting, offering a choice between flat mids, a moderate cut, or a deep notch. Originally released as a limited collaboration with Obstructures as the 0xEAE Bass Driver, the Greathammer standardizes the design into a compact enclosure with external controls and silent electronic switching. Electronic Audio Experiments browse by type volume/amplification amplification preamp / clean boost browse by type distortion/fuzz/overdrive overdrive browse by enclosure pedal Electronic Audio Experiments Greathammer - Solidstate Bass Drive Published on January 29, 2026 Electronic Audio Experiments boost / preamp overdrive pedal Information The Electronic Audio Experiments Greathammer is a bass-focused solid-state overdrive and preamp designed to deliver aggressive, articulate grind with extended low-frequency authority. Inspired by a beloved 1970s Canadian solid-state bass amplifier known for its bright, piano-like attack, the Greathammer preserves the core character that later became a defining element of 90s noise rock while substantially expanding the usable tonal range. Entire circuit blocks were redesigned from the ground up to retain articulation and impact while supporting more restrained, balanced tones as well as extreme, saturated sounds suited for down-tuned and high-output applications. The Greathammer is an evolution of the Electronic Audio Experiments 0xEAE Bass Driver, originally released in Spring 2025. For the Greathammer, the circuit was updated to fit a standard pedalboard-friendly enclosure, the previously internal mid-notch switch was moved to the exterior, and a significantly quieter electronic bypass switching scheme was implemented. These revisions preserved the core voice of the earlier design while improving usability, flexibility, and integration into modern pedalboards. At the heart of the Greathammer is a solid-state signal path built around a multi-band transistor clipping circuit derived from the classic tri-comp topology. This clipping stage splits the signal into multiple frequency bands and clips each independently, producing a complex, harmonically rich distortion with a pronounced, percussive attack. A high-headroom op amp input stage provides up to approximately 50 dB of gain, allowing the pedal to function anywhere from clean boost to extreme overdrive. The input and output are both buffered with high-fidelity op amps, ensuring consistent performance anywhere in the signal chain and enabling silent electronic switching. sources.bodyExcerpt: Model feT — Electronic Audio Experiments Pedals Accessories DIY Dealers Blog Support About Menu Pedals Accessories DIY Dealers Blog Support About × Filter All Pedals ← Back to Pedals Model feT Temporarily Unavailable Model feT $249.00 The Model feT is a transistor-based preamplifier designed around the legendary Sunn Model T amplifier. Those who have played the original know that while it excels at heavy tones when pushed, it is far more than just an amp for stoner rock and doom metal. In fact, on its own it is a fantastic mid-gain amplifier with a tone that is dark, yet clear and present—making it an exceptional pedal platform. Most famous Model T tones come from putting a distortion or fuzz in front of the amp. Thus, the Model feT is designed to sound good on its own and with other pedals stacked in front. This pedal goes beyond the standard triode-to-JFET emulation approach with the inclusion of an emulated power amp. This broadens the range of gain and—in the true spirit of the original amp—allows for massive headroom and volume output. This greatly expands its capabilities beyond a typical drive pedal: the Model feT can be used directly into a power amp, cab simulation, or DAW. Finish: Select Finish Raw Aluminum Slate Gray Concrete Sparkle Acid Etch Smoke Swirl Raw Aluminum Slate Gray Concrete Sparkle Acid Etch Smoke Swirl Add To Cart Electrical Specifications Bypass: Relay switching with true bypass Input impedance @ 1 Khz: 500kΩ Output impedance @ 1 Khz: 1kΩ Power: 9V DC, 2.1 mm center negative barrel. The current draw is 65 mA . We recommend a regulated, isolated power supply rated for 100 mA minimum. Our pedals do not accept batteries. Use of an incorrect power supply may cause permanent damage. Download manual Controls Normal: turn clockwise to add gain from the parallel “Normal” channel, which has a neutral voicing. Higher settings produce a thicker gain sound. The normal channel is fully muted when this control is at zero. Brite: turn clockwise to add gain from the parallel “Brite” channel, which is voiced for extra midrange and sparkle. Adds bite to the drive tone at higher settings. The “Brite” channel is fully muted when this control is at zero. Bass, Midrange, Treble : 3-band FMV EQ with the same moderately mid-scooped voicing as the original amp: highly interactive and nonlinear, but familiar. Master: sets overall output volume. This control is capable of high volumes in order to access quieter clean settings and to properly drive an external power amp. Electronic Audio Experiments browse by type volume/amplification amplification preamp / clean boost browse by enclosure pedal Electronic Audio Experiments Model feT - Model T Preamp Published on July 13, 2017 Electronic Audio Experiments boost / preamp pedal dragon's blood dragon's blood dragon's blood red dragon's blood dragon's blood red dragon's blood Information Electronic Audio Experiments The Model feT is a transistor-based preamplifier designed around the legendary Sunn Model T amplifier. Those who have played the original know that while it excels at heavy tones when pushed, it is far more just an amp for stoner rock and doom metal. In fact, on its own it is a rather clean amplifier with a tone that is dark, yet clear and present. Most famous Model T tones come from putting a distortion or fuzz in front of the amp. Thus, the Model feT is designed to sound good on its own and with other pedals stacked into it. This pedal goes beyond the standard triode-to-JFET conversion to deliver massive headroom and volume output, in the true spirit of the amp which inspired it. And finally, the Model feT can be used straight into a power amp, greatly expanding its capabilities beyond that of a typical drive pedal. Controls: Independent gain controls for the Normal and Brite channels 3-band EQ with the same voicing as the original amp Master volume This pedal has the standard I/O complement: true bypass, 9V center negative power, top-mounted jacks. All Model feT pedals come with the standard warranty. Instead of locking you into a single flavour of overdrive, it lets you shape the harmonic structure that determines how a drive sounds and responds. Add to Cart Testimonials [The Empress Drive] is like super super amp-like, and I don't mean that in a like "everybody says it". It feels like you're playing a cranked amp. Sounds awesome. — Josh Scott, JHS Pedals The Empress Drive is seriously one of the most versatile overdrives I have tried to date. You can transform your clean amp into a very angry tweed Deluxe, or use it as a flamethrower with all the gain it has on tap. PLUS even if it did absolutely nothing the aesthetic is totally worth the price of admission. — Ben Flanders (MD/Guitarist for Ella Langley) I really appreciate the EQ. Most drives have a tone dial, but the degree to which you can EQ your sound with this pedal is special. The BASS, MIDRANGE, TREBLE, MID FREQ, MIX, and GAIN dials invite sonic exploration. A wide variety of sonic possibilities can be created. This pedal allows guitarists to sculpt a custom sound. It's fantastic! — Donna Grantis (Prince, 3RDEYEGIRL) It sounds sooo good!!! The main drive sounds natural and just perfect to my ears :) Then being able to customize is awesome, with the Mid Freq sweep that’s pleasing across the spectrum. The gate works smoothly too, there are no weird cut-outs or change in tone. The dry signal mix is so useful for many situations, and I love that it sounds clear and natural. — Barbie Almalbis Honasan Empress' new Drive box makes my BassBot 303 clone sound like Jimmy Page! like when his bowing technique makes your skin shiver, just enough grit, just enough overtone, just enough boost. — Andrew Whiteman (Broken Social Scene) Features Tube-like overdrive with advanced tone control Sweepable Midrange for precise harmonic shaping Mix control to preserve your amp’s natural breakup Active Bass and Treble shelving filters Up to 30 dB of pre- or post-clipping, footswitchable boost Built-in analog clipping meter with selectable LED colour Adaptive noise gate Breakup Control Most overdrives shape tone after distortion. Empress Effects browse by type distortion/fuzz/overdrive overdrive browse by enclosure pedal Empress Effects Drive Published on May 5, 2026 Empress Effects overdrive pedal Information The Empress Effects Drive is an all-analog overdrive pedal that provides direct control over how its clipping stage responds, focusing on shaping harmonic content rather than applying fixed voicing. Its design centers on a pre-overdrive midrange stage that determines which frequencies drive the clipping process, allowing the user to influence saturation behavior, articulation, and harmonic density before distortion occurs. The circuit originated from combining a discontinued Germ Drive design with elements from another high-gain circuit, followed by iterative refinement of clipping options and EQ placement to improve responsiveness and versatility. The result is not modeled after a specific amplifier, but instead offers a range of gain textures through parameter interaction. A sweepable midrange control, paired with a dedicated mid-frequency selector, operates ahead of the clipping stage. Adjusting this section changes which frequencies push the circuit into saturation, altering the resulting harmonic structure and dynamic response. This differs from conventional post-distortion tone shaping by affecting how the overdrive is generated rather than how it is filtered afterward. Signal blending is handled by a parallel mix control, allowing the dry input to be combined with the overdriven signal to retain clarity and transient detail. After this stage, active bass and treble shelving filters shape the combined signal, maintaining consistent frequency balance regardless of blend settings. An integrated boost circuit provides up to 30 dB of additional gain and can be assigned either before the overdrive stage or after it. In pre-overdrive mode, it increases saturation and compression by driving the clipping stage harder, while also applying filtering to control low-frequency buildup. In post-overdrive mode, it raises the overall output level without altering the distortion character. The pedal includes an adaptive noise gate that monitors the input signal and adjusts its threshold dynamically, reducing noise during high-gain operation while preserving sustain and note decay. All returns accepted within 45 days of purchase User Manual English French German Spanish Support The Heavy Menace is the most versatile distortion pedal that Empress Effects has ever created. It’s an evolution of the original Heavy with new features and a compact enclosure. In addition to the original Heavy and Heavier modes, the Heavy Menace adds a new Lite(ish) mode, covering any high-gain sound from classic hard rock to searing modern metal. Add to Cart Features Three versatile distortion modes - Lite(ish), Heavy, and Heavier Footswitchable noise gate Three-band EQ with sweepable mid frequency Weight control to sculpt low frequency response Linked or independent switching of the distortion and gate Gate key input (⅛” TS or TRS) True bypass or buffered bypass Artists who use Heavy Menace Chris Wrate ENHANCED EQ We’re obsessed with EQ, and the 3-band circuit on Heavy Menace is one of our best. Our Weight control adjusts a high-pass filter in the distortion circuit to shape low-end character. Turn it up for a thick, full sound, or turn counterclockwise for a tight response that’s perfect for palm muting and extended-range guitars. Midrange is a key element of a great distorted sound, so the mid frequency is sweepable from 200 Hz to 2.5 kHz to dial in the sweet spot for your guitar and amp. Scoop for a tight, aggressive sound, or push to add definition and cut through a mix. TRUE OR BUFFERED BYPASS The Heavy Menace offers both true bypass for maximum transparency, and buffered bypass to protect against signal loss over long cable runs. ADAPTIVE GATE Players loved the gate on the original Heavy. Envelope followers in the circuit respond to your playing, letting sustained notes decay naturally but clamping down quickly during fast stops. On the Heavy Menace, this gate is now footswitchable, with two available modes of operation. In normal bypass mode, the gate doesn’t affect the signal if the distortion is off, while independent bypass mode is like having separate distortion and gate pedals. We’ve also added a key input so you can optionally trigger the gate with an external signal. This is particularly useful if you have additional pedals before the Heavy Menace in your signal chain, such as a low-gain pedal for stacking. Split a clean signal with a pedal like our Buffer+ and connect it to the Gate Key Input, and the gate will behave consistently regardless of changes at the main input. The ~900 (About Nine Hundred) is Fairfield's flagship fuzz, a spiritual successor to their discontinued Four Eyes. Two cascading JFET gain stages create thick, harmonically rich fuzz with serious sustain. The circuit maintains note definition even at maximum saturation, avoiding the woolly mush that plagues lesser fuzzes. Fairfield's Quebec workshop produces these by hand with their characteristic attention to detail. The ~900 represents their vision of what modern fuzz should be. sources.title: Fairfield Circuitry The Unpleasant Surprise Demo Review | Loopy Demos
sources.description: Fairfield Circuitry The Unpleasant Surprise: an experimental fuzz and gate pedal with Volume, Onset and T, G, C toggles for gritty, gated, chaotic fuzz tones.
sources.snippet: Fairfield Circuitry The Unpleasant Surprise Demo Review
sources.bodyExcerpt: --> Fairfield Circuitry The Unpleasant Surprise Demo Review | Loopy Demos Show or hide the side bar navigation Loopy Demos Demos Posts Manufacturers About Contact Demos Posts Manufacturers About Contact All demos Fairfield Circuitry The Unpleasant Surprise Apr 15, 2024 Read next What is the Best Velcro Fuzz Pedal? The Unpleasant Surprise by Fairfield Circuitry earns its ominous name honestly. It’s an experimental fuzz and gate, in the builder’s own words, built for jarring, textured, occasionally chaotic tones rather than a polite gain boost. The control set is refreshingly compact for what it does: two knobs and three toggles swing the pedal from tight, controllable fuzz into sputtery, gated chaos and back again. It rewards exploring by ear rather than dialing in a spec sheet, which is very much the point. Controls VOLUME comes first, setting output level with unity gain around noon, plenty on tap to slam whatever comes next in the chain. ONSET sits beside it and is the real character knob: Fairfield’s manual describes it as interstage gain that mimics an inverse gate threshold, so turning it up brings more saturation and longer sustain, while turning it down drops into sputtery, ad-lib territory bordering on gating out entirely. Below the knobs sit three 2-way toggles: T, G and C, all shaping fuzz character rather than gain staging. T is a simple output treble cut. G affects the amplifier’s bias, moving between a more open and a more saturated voicing, though the difference narrows as ONSET climbs. C is a feedforward stage that crushes the signal, with ONSET controlling how much compression stacks on it, and it’s the toggle most responsible for the pedal’s harshest, most splattered textures. In the demo above I’ve set up sweeps for Onset, T, G and C, so you can hear each control on its own before working through the presets. How It Sounds Velcro Fuzz keeps Onset low at 3 with C flipped in for crush while T and G sit at base, giving a choppy, velcro-textured decay that stutters rather than sustains. Raunchy Drive drops Onset further to 1.5, deep in the sputtery range the manual describes, flipping T and G to their other positions with C’s crush still engaged for a rawer, more open drive. Blistering Splatter and Super Octave share the same T, G and C combination; the only difference is Onset, at 3 and 5 respectively, and that extra saturation in Super Octave pushes the harmonics into the upper, octave-like register the name promises. Weird Wonderful raises Onset to 6 with T flipped for treble cut, G and C back at base, sitting between gated chaos and the smoother end of the range. Thick Fuzz maxes Onset at 10 with G and C engaged, right where the manual points for the most saturation and sustain, and it sounds it: dense, compressed and thick throughout. The Unpleasant Surprise vs ZVEX Fuzz Factory The ZVEX Fuzz Factory is the other gated, unpredictable fuzz on this site, so it’s the obvious cross-shop. The Fuzz Factory gets its chaos from five interacting knobs (Volume, Gate, Comp, Drive, Stab) built around germanium transistors, squealing and self-oscillating the further Gate and Stab push against each other. The Unpleasant Surprise reaches similar gated, chaotic territory a different way: two knobs and three toggles, with ONSET doing double duty as gain and gate threshold. It’s a more contained kind of unpredictable, but the same appetite for happy accidents: the Fuzz Factory for maximum interactive chaos, the Unpleasant Surprise for strange, ugly territory from a simpler control set. There’s also a side by side page for this one: Fairfield Circuitry Unpleasant Surprise vs ZVEX Fuzz Factory , both pedals on the same loop so you can switch between them mid-phrase. Who It’s For This is a pedal for garage rock, noise, experimental and psych players who want a fuzz that occasionally bites back rather than a boutique gain stage tuned for polite tone, whether as a chaotic solo voice or flipped on to turn a clean section upside dow

Sku: FAIRFIELDTUS Brand: Fairfield Circuitry Fairfield Circuitry The Unpleasant Surprise - Experimental Fuzz/Gate Reminisce about the time you got your shoulder caught in the reciprocating saw while this unit destroys your slick jazz lines. The fruit of an oddball circuit, hanging there awkwardly by some parasitic effect. Tweaked, bended and shoe-horned to optimize it's stench, it's unpleasance. Time has come to turn all dynamics to shit. Strangely, it feels very natural. As The Unpleasant Surprise turns your playing style upside down, you’ll be thankful for its ability to push you outside the box, outside your comfort zone, all the while retaining the essence of what is played. The artifacts created by this pedal are strange, harsh and unusual but never seem mis - placed or out of context. About Fairfield Circuitry Founded in 2008, Fairfield Circuitry and creator Guillaume Fairfield have had an unquestionable impact on the FX pedal category. Multiple hits like Shallow Water, Randy’s Revenge, and the Barbershop have earned a long-standing reputation for some of the most known and uniquely notable boutique pedals produced to date. A simplistic almost brutalist design aesthetic seemingly dares the user to discover the electronic creativity within each unit. Users find ground-breaking interpretations of both classic and unusual sounds emanating throughout the entire catalogue. Fairfield Circuitry is based in Quebec, Canada. sources.bodyExcerpt: Review: Fender Hammertone Distortion - Mixdown Magazine READING Review: Fender Hammertone Distortion Subscribe X Subscribe to Mixdown Magazine Select State NSW QLD VIC ACT TAS SA WA NT --> Subscribe News Features Reviews Directory Giveaways Videos Magazines Privacy & Policies Advertise Contact Terms & Conditions Reviews 28.06.2022 Review: Fender Hammertone Distortion Words by Luke Shields Fender Australia | Price: $159 Not to gloat, dear reader, but I consider myself pretty lucky where gear ownership is concerned. Many of the sundry pedals spilling wantonly from both my go-to board and the drawers, shelves, and cupboard under the stairs where my cast-offs go were given to me by people who, misguidedly or otherwise, believed that I would use them wisely to make something of myself. The joke’s on them I guess, but I digress. Read more product reviews here. Like most guitar players who took up the sword any time in the last 30 years, my naive desire to look, be, and sound like Kurt Cobain was what set my fingers twitching all those years ago. With that in mind, my most coveted gift suggestion as a 14-or-so-year-old was a distortion pedal, really ANY distortion pedal, to plug in between my student pack guitar and amp and shred four chords at a time forever and ever, amen. One glorious Christian-come-Capitalist holiday, I unceremoniously unboxed what I later discovered had been affectionately dubbed ‘the worst distortion pedal ever’ and I was hooked. Every wishlist thereafter was incomplete without one noisemaker or another in prime position to add to my first, monotonal box of rock. Among effects, distortion has reigned supreme for the better part of a century. While clean tones bejewelled by lush time-based effects are enjoying another little bit of a renaissance of late, it shows no sign of relinquishing the throne, particularly for players looking for their first footswitch to fiddle with. Enter Fender’s new Hammertone Distortion in all its bristling, hefty glory. The Hammertone line assumes an interesting place in Fender’s product line. At first glance, one could be forgiven for glossing over these austere, grey boxes, assuming that they are merely another smattering of the most mass appeal, oft-requested sounds as trotted out by just about everyone who has ever picked up a soldering iron. Au contraire, while there is indeed one of each of the main branches of the effect family tree present, their designers have made a point of sitting them just a little to the left of centre in the personality department. Attempting to make simple pleasures anew is thin ice that companies both great and small have fallen through time and time again. However, I am now four pedals deep in the lineup and have not been disappointed or thoroughly un-surprised yet. The Hammertone Distortion is a prime example of that rubric. It has everything that the current trend towards ’90s revivalism dictates but with more range than you might expect. For the most part, it is pitched toward the more bass-heavy, gutsier end of the frequency spectrum, meaning that it should play well alongside Soviet-style fuzzes and the ilk with the greatest of ease. It is chiefly there to deliver a goliath, bristling wall of sound at the crest of the gain dial, ripe for all those groove-laden drop D riffs you’ve been itching to show the band in the week between jams. From there, I was also able to pull a fairly palatable, fiery, nasal, HM2-style squawk out of it, which is a commendable amount of range for something designed to be driven that hard. From Earth to Entombed in one fell swoop is no mean feat! Adding hair and punch to a roaring wave of gain is without a doubt its primary function, but like all good Fender fans, I wanted to know how it handled in the softer moments. While it didn’t quite pare back to Klon-style transparent overdrive territory, I was pleased to meet quite a handsome torn speaker sound at the lower end of the sweep which could be a tast

sources.bodyExcerpt: Fender Hammertone Distortion | Delicious Audio Creative Pedals Creative Delay Tape Delay W/ Reverb Delay Distortion Fuzz Overdrive Dual Gain Dirt Boost Compr. + Dynamics Dynamics EQ Filter Wah Filter+EQ Lo-Fi 8 Bit Lo-fi Chorus Flanger Phaser Tremolo Uni-Vibe Modulation Pitch Shifter Octaver pitch Multiverb Reverb Spring Reverb Reverb CV In Granular Synth Pedals Synth Effect Guides Monthly Lists Shopping Guides Coverage Schedule Facebook Stompbox Exhibit Fender Hammertone Distortion Updated Aug. 3, 2022 | by Paolo De Gregorio The Fender Hammertone Distortion is one-ninth of the new affordable line of pedals released by the electric guitar giant in early 2022. The US company’s 2018 Pugilist distortion was very well received (and it’s currently on top of our article about the best distortion pedals ) but we don’t know if this $80 pedal inherits anything from that circuit. The pedal’s look and layout is rather generic and – frankly – unremarkable (c’mon Fender, a better font ain’t going to break the bank, is it?), with knobs for Level, Gain, and active EQ controls for Treble and Bass. Under the hood, a mid-range trim pot lets you add bite and bark, while a tone control lets you roll off super-high frequencies to taylor the pedal to your amp. Have a listen to how it sounds in the videos below. Fender Hammertone Distortion, Builder’s Notes The sound of rock’n’roll – from light drive to heavy crunch, guitar wouldn’t be the same without it. The Hammertone™ Distortion delivers the legendary distorted tones you need for nearly any style of music. The active 2-band Bass and Treble EQ controls provide modern tone-shaping flexibility, while the pedal board-friendly top-mounted in out jacks and true bypass footswitch mean it will integrate seamlessly into your rig. FEATURES Fender®-Designed Analog Distortion Circuit 2-Band Active Bass Treble EQ Top Mount Input/Output Jacks True-Bypass Switching Powered by 9-Volt Battery or Center Negative AC Adaptor, Not Included ORIGINAL FENDER®-DESIGNED DISTORTION CIRCUIT Designed by our in-house experts, the Hammertone™ Distortion is a low-noise, high-power rock machine with a dynamic and versatile sound. ACTIVE EQ CONTROLS Active Bass and Treble controls provide massive control over your tone, with up to 15db of boost or cut. INTERNAL TONE CONTROLS The internal trim-pot controls allow for pre-set adjustments to further shape your sound. A mid-range trimmer lets you add bite and bark, while the tone control allows you to dial down super-high frequencies to tame your amp. CUSTOM COLOR “F” LOGO KNOBS Paying homage to Fender’s historic custom colors, these “F” logo knobs are easy to read, easy to grip and stand out on stage. RUGGED, ROAD-WORTHY HARDWARE The rugged aluminum enclosure and metal hardware deliver road-worthy reliability. True bypass switching ensure easy setup and pure tone. TOP-MOUNT JACKS Top-mounted input and output jacks allow more pedals to be used on the same board, as well as increasing pedal routing options. sources.description: The Fender MTG Tube Distortion pedal delivers authentic tube-driven distortion in a compact format. Featuring a NOS 6205 preamp tube, 3-band EQ, and a Tight control, it offers versatile tone shaping. A footswitchable boost with independent level and gain controls adds further flexibility. Co-designed with Bruce Egnater, this pedal provides the classic Fender look with LED-backlit knobs and a durable aluminum chassis, making it a must-have for guitarists seeking true tube breakup. Consider this as an alternative to other distortion pedals like the [Proco RAT](/pedals/proco-rat).

What Fender say about the MTG Tube Distortion Overview AUTHENTIC TUBE TONE Many pedals try to emulate the sound of tube breakup; we decided instead of emulating tube distortion, we'd use actual vacuum tubes and give you the real deal in a compact pedal. The heart of the MTG's design is a NOS (New Old Stock) US-made 6205 preamp tube. 3-Band EQ with Tight control and switchable boost - with its own Level and Boost controls - makes it easy to dial-in just the right sound.
